headline: This blueprint maps the U.S. federal AML/CFT program-establishment (pillars) regime as of a pinned 2026 date: a statutory base duty implemented in parallel by four federal banking agencies, FinCEN's sector-specific rules, and the FINRA SRO layer, alongside examiner guidance and pending modernization NPRMs.
how_to_read: Items are grouped by family: statute (31-usc-*, amla-2020-uncodified), regulation_fba (OCC/Fed/FDIC/NCUA program rules), regulation_fincen (31 CFR 1010/1020/1022/1023), sro_rule_guidance (FINRA Rule 3310, CAB 331, and FINRA notices/FAQs), exam_manual (FFIEC manual sections), guidance_fincen/guidance_fba (agency and SR-letter guidance), horizon_rulemaking (proposed NPRM text, obligations intentionally empty), and enforcement_index (evidence-only, no obligations extracted). Each item's evidence_role marks its evidentiary weight — binding_authority and sro_rule binding text sit above agency_guidance/supervisory_guidance, which sit above enforcement_evidence and horizon, which never state operative duties. Obligation rows carry their own modal tag ([must]/[must_not]/[should]/[may]/[conditional]) taken verbatim from the source's own verb, not harmonized across sources. The defect register (D1–D10 codes) records described frictions — duplication, divergence, dangling references, undefined terms, gaps, obsolescence, scattering, and scope mismatches — each tied to item_ids; every highlight and tension below points back to those refs rather than asserting a resolved position.

regime_shape.heading: Statutory spine
regime_shape.text: 31 U.S.C. 5311, 5312, 5318, and 5334, together with the uncodified Division F provisions of AMLA 2020, supply the generic base duty that 'each financial institution shall establish' a risk-based AML/CFT program, the Secretary's authority to set minimum standards and exemptions, the concentration-account and priorities provisions, and the examiner-training duty. The pillars duty here is stated at the level of 'financial institution' generically, with sector-specific content left to implementing regulations.

regime_shape.heading: Federal banking-agency layer
regime_shape.text: The OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA each maintain a parallel BSA compliance-program rule (12 CFR 21.21, 208.63, 326.8, 748.2) stating the same four minimum program contents — internal controls, independent testing, a designated compliance coordinator, and training — plus a conditional CIP component tied to 31 U.S.C. 5318(l) and its implementing regulation, written/board-approved/minuted in near-identical language across the four instruments.

regime_shape.heading: FinCEN sector-specific rules and CDD layer
regime_shape.text: FinCEN's Part 1010 general provisions, Part 1020 (banks), Part 1022 (MSBs), and Part 1023 (broker-dealers) each restate a program-establishment obligation tailored to that sector, and the CDD rule (1010.230, echoed in 1010) layers on a due-diligence program covering correspondent accounts, private banking accounts, the foreign-shell-bank prohibition, and beneficial ownership, incorporated by cross-reference into the bank and broker-dealer program rules.

regime_shape.heading: FINRA SRO layer for broker-dealers
regime_shape.text: For broker-dealers, 31 CFR 1023.210(c) makes SEC-effective SRO AML-program rules a compliance component of the federal duty; FINRA Rule 3310 and Capital Acquisition Broker Rule 331 supply the operative SRO-layer pillars (written program, senior-management approval, detection/reporting policies, independent testing, designated AML compliance person, training, fifth-pillar CDD), which are then restated across a dense set of FINRA regulatory notices, FAQs, and the annual oversight report.

regime_shape.heading: Supervisory guidance and horizon rulemaking
regime_shape.text: The FFIEC examination manual restates and elaborates the banking-agency pillars for examiner use (risk assessment, internal controls, independent testing, compliance officer, training, program structures), largely in 'should' rather than 'must' language, while FinCEN and OCC/Fed guidance items (including the AML/CFT national priorities and two pending NPRMs from 2024 and 2026) describe a proposed modernization of the program rules that has not taken binding effect as of the pinned date.

regime_shape.heading: Enforcement evidence at the edge
regime_shape.text: Enforcement indices for FinCEN, the federal banking agencies, and SEC/FINRA/CFTC are retained as evidence-only sources under the ratified scope: they document that program-establishment expectations are applied in practice but state no operative obligations themselves, and one item was found to contain no in-scope program content at all.

highlights.point: 31 U.S.C. 5318(h) is the load-bearing statutory node: nearly every sector rule (banking-agency, FinCEN bank/MSB/broker-dealer, FINRA) is built by tracing back to its generic 'each financial institution shall establish' duty, but the sector-specific content is assembled only by reading the statute together with implementing regulations and SRO rules, not stated in any single instrument.

The four-pillar program content (internal controls, independent testing, designated compliance officer, training) is restated in materially identical language across the OCC, Federal Reserve, FDIC, and NCUA rules, making these four instruments a dense duplicate cluster rather than four independent regimes.

FINRA Rule 3310 functions as the anchor instrument for the entire broker-dealer/SRO layer: its program pillars are restated across at least six separate FINRA notices, FAQs, and the annual oversight report, and the CAB Rule 331 track largely mirrors it for capital acquisition brokers.

The Customer Identification Program requirement is a cross-sector pillar appearing in near-parallel form for banks (31 CFR 1020.220) and broker-dealers (31 CFR 1023.220), including minimum identifying information, verification timing, terrorist-list screening, and five-year recordkeeping — a heavily load-bearing, densely cross-referenced obligation set.

The MSB program rule (31 CFR 1022.210) is a dense node in its own right, generating FinCEN guidance on agent monitoring, foreign agent/counterparty due diligence, and independent review — each restating the same core AML-program duty from a different angle.

The FinCEN AML/CFT national priorities (issued 2021 under 31 U.S.C. 5318(h)(4)) are a hub that every covered-institution risk-based program is expected to review and incorporate, but the item's own notes flag that no update has issued within the statutory four-year cycle as of the pinned 2026 date.

Two pending Notices of Proposed Rulemaking (OCC 2024 and 2026, plus FinCEN's own 2026 program-modernization NPRM) describe a prospective restructuring of the pillars rules to add national-priorities consideration and CDD incorporation, but under the evidentiary ceiling none of this proposed content is an operative duty.

tensions.point: The term 'financial institution' — the duty-holder for the entire pillars regime — is defined differently across the corpus: 31 U.S.C. 5312(a)(2)'s enumerated list versus AMLA 2020's expanded definition incorporating additional categories, a divergence that runs through 5311, 5318, and the uncodified AMLA text.

Multiple current banking-agency and statutory instruments still cross-reference the superseded 31 CFR Part 103 numbering (and specific dead cites like 103.121) rather than the recodified 31 CFR Chapter X, while sibling instruments in the same corpus use the updated citations.

The CDD 'fifth pillar' (ongoing due diligence, beneficial ownership, customer risk profile) is an explicit program element in FinCEN's Part 1020/1023 rules and in FINRA Rule 3310/CAB 331, but is not present as program-establishment content in the federal banking-agency pillars rules themselves, even though a pending NPRM would add it there.

Independent-testing frequency and scope thresholds diverge across instruments governing the same pillar: FINRA's annual/biennial framework, CAB Rule 331's flat two-year cadence, the MSB rule's risk-commensurate standard, and the FFIEC manual's non-mandatory 'no regulatory requirement' framing all describe the same functional obligation differently.

31 CFR 1022.210 contains an internal tension: agent-only MSBs and their principals may contractually allocate responsibility for program elements, while the same section simultaneously provides that each MSB remains solely and non-relievably responsible for program implementation.

Board-approval and program-availability requirements apply unevenly across sectors: banking-agency rules require board approval and minuting for all covered institutions, while FinCEN's Part 1020 imposes explicit board-approval/FinCEN-availability duties only on banks lacking a Federal functional regulator, and broker-dealer/MSB rules use different approval actors (senior management vs. board/governing body).

The complete program-establishment obligation for banks and for broker-dealers is not stated in any single instrument in either case; it must be assembled by reading the base statutory duty together with sector CFR provisions, the CIP rule, and (for broker-dealers) SRO rules — yet no FINRA/SRO rule content of the kind 1023.210(c) requires is present in the FinCEN regulation extraction itself.

The statutory duty to update AML/CFT priorities at least every four years and the parallel duty to incorporate those priorities into risk-based programs are both described as currently unmet or deferred: the 2021 priorities have not been refreshed, and the incorporation/examination mechanism is expressly deferred to future regulations that are not yet final.

The two pending OCC NPRMs (2024 and 2026) and the FinCEN 2026 NPRM describe overlapping modernization efforts but frame the acting agency group inconsistently (four agencies versus three, with the Federal Reserve's role unclear in the later document) and cite the underlying statutory subparagraph differently for banks/broker-dealers versus MSBs.

caveats: This summary describes the blueprint and defect register as given; it does not settle, harmonize, or evaluate any of the tensions listed, which remain open for Phase 3 governance. Enforcement-index items (evidence_role: enforcement_evidence) and the horizon NPRM items (evidence_role: horizon, status: horizon) are cited only to show that expectations exist or are proposed; nothing from those items is stated here as an operative duty. One enforcement item (enf-index-sec-finra-cftc-aml-enforcement) is flagged nothing_in_scope and contributes no obligations or definitions. SAR/CTR/CDD identification specifics, OFAC/sanctions, fraud, state AML/licensing, and other covered sectors are boundary/coordination matters under the ratified scope and are referenced only where a defect item or note in the digest itself documents an absence or interaction, never asserted as independently established facts.
